description: I’m a BS AI student at ITU Lahore with hands-on experience in machine learning, Kaggle competitions, and building shipped apps. I want to apply those skills to real space and Earth-science data, work with a team under a tight deadline, and learn how NASA’s open datasets are used to solve real problems.
summary: IGNIS LAB is a web dashboard built for two groups: the people who design and protect future crew habitats (spacecraft fire-safety engineers, and the researchers who decide which experiment NASA flies next), and students and space enthusiasts who want to discover how fire behaves without gravity. It summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA's microgravity combustion research. Its Atlas ranks all 24 combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository for the cabin air a crew will breathe: today's ISS, a lunar habitat, or NASA's oxygen-rich exploration atmosphere (8.2 psia, 34% O2), counting the real tests NASA ran near each one. Predict uses models trained on 274 droplet fires burned on the ISS (FLEX) to estimate whether a flame goes out early and how fast it burns, beside the five closest real NASA runs; a GREEN/AMBER/RED check withholds the numbers wherever the data runs out. For learners, a 3D Fire lab shows a candle flame turning into a dim blue ball when gravity disappears and burns a droplet with the real model. A Safety page and cited answers from NASA's own reports complete it. This matters because NASA plans oxygen-rich air for future habitats, yet FLEX has no droplet tests near that atmosphere: IGNIS LAB makes such gaps visible and shows where new experiments are needed.
details:
Live app: https://ignis-lab.streamlit.app

Code: https://github.com/WingManOO7/ignis-lab

WHO IT IS FOR

Spacecraft fire-safety engineers and the researchers who decide which experiment NASA flies next, plus students and space enthusiasts who want to see how fire behaves without gravity.

THE PROBLEM

NASA plans oxygen-rich air (34% O2) for future habitats, and fire in a sealed cabin is unforgiving: Apollo 1 burned in pure oxygen. NASA's microgravity fire data is open, but it is spread across 24 investigations, so it is hard to see which experiments apply to a habitat or where the evidence runs out.

THE 3D FIRE LAB (OUR HIGHLIGHT)

An interactive 3D journey that shows why fire behaves differently in space, driven by real NASA data:

- Earth lab: a candle burns as a yellow teardrop; switch gravity off and it becomes a dim blue sphere, because hot air no longer rises.

- Orbit and cabin: fly to a spacecraft and step inside, where smoke cannot rise to a ceiling detector.

- NASA's FLEX chamber: every slider (fuel, oxygen, pressure, CO2, droplet size) runs our trained models live in the browser. The droplet shrinks at the predicted burning rate and goes out where the nearest NASA runs did; outside NASA's tested conditions it shows "not simulated" instead of guessing.

- Wiring fire by the fan (illustrative, based on NASA's Saffire tests): spark the wires, the fan feeds the fire, fan off starves it into a blue ball, more oxygen makes it flash, and CO2 puts it out while the smoke stays.

- A narrator and a "Play the story" tour guide you through it; every element is labelled DATA or ILLUSTRATIVE, and it works offline.

THE REST OF THE APP

- Atlas: ranks all 24 NASA PSI combustion investigations for ISS, lunar or exploration air, counting real tests near each. FLEX has 0 droplet tests near the exploration atmosphere: a clear research gap.

- Predict: models trained on 274 ISS droplet fires (FLEX) estimate whether a flame goes out early and how fast it burns, beside the 5 closest real NASA runs; a GREEN/AMBER/RED light withholds numbers where the data runs out.

- Trust: grouped cross-validation against baselines (Brier score 0.074 vs 0.115 for guessing); our refit of NASA's raw droplet data matches NASA within a 2.3% median.

- Safety page (detection, suppression, extinguishers, lessons from past fires) and Ask (cited answers from 8 NASA reports, with an optional checked Gemini answer).

IMPACT

Engineers see what NASA's data covers and where not to trust it; researchers get the gaps and the next experiment to fly (droplet tests in exploration air); learners can explore fire in microgravity hands-on. It is a decision-support tool, not a certification tool.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scope (models cover isolated FLEX droplets only), no data leakage between tests, calibrated probabilities, plain language, offline 3D, no NASA logos, CC0 NASA data, SI use disclosed in the README.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, Streamlit, Plotly, pytest), JavaScript with three.js, Google Gemini API, Streamlit Community Cloud, GitHub.
